title: Portland's Adult Soap Box Derby: Where Gravity Meets Glitter and a Giant Sloth Head
summary:
Gravity is an inescapable force—it keeps our atmosphere in place and our feet on the ground. But in Portland, Oregon, gravity is also the engine for one of the most gloriously unhinged races in America: the Adult Soap Box Derby. On August 15, 42 homemade cars hurtled down the slopes of Mt. Tabor, an extinct volcano, in the event's 27th year. Unlike the streamlined, speed-obsessed soap box derbies for kids, Portland's version is a chaotic fusion of art installation, block party, and downhill dash.

The cars are the stars. This year's lineup included a giant sloth head, a Zamboni themed after a hockey rivalry called "The Ice Melter," a replica of the Flintstones' foot-powered car, and a car depicting Oregon's infamous exploding whale. John Nurse built a dragon car based on a drawing by his 10-year-old, using hula hoops, spray foam, and the chassis of a 1979 Honda Odyssey ATV. "How many times do you get to race a dragon down a volcano?" he asked. The derby has minimal rules—helmets, brakes, and basic safety training—but beyond that, it's a free-for-all of wood, metal, plastic, fake fur, and hot-glued mirror tiles.

The event's history stretches back to the 1930s, when soap box racing became a national institution. But Portland's version, which began in 1997, has always prioritized pageantry over speed. "It's basically a party that Portland throws for itself every year," said David Paulsen, the derby's president, who fell in love with the event after his first visit. He affectionately described the cars as "booger-welded garbage cars racing down a mountain." Several thousand spectators turned out with folding chairs and blankets, cheering for hours. Brittany England, creator of the Rocky Roadster ice cream truck car, captured the vibe: "There's so many people, the vibes are great, the energy's awesome." In a world of high-tech racing, Portland's derby proves that sometimes the best vehicle is the one that makes you laugh.
why_it_matters: Local traditions like this matter because they show that public space can be used for creativity, humor, and belonging rather than just winning. For a teenager, it is a reminder that organized fun can be experimental and that a community's identity is built through the stories it tells about itself.

background_read: In the 1930s, soap box racing grew from a backyard pastime into a national youth institution, with communities holding downhill races for homemade, engine-free cars.
Portland's Mt. Tabor—an extinct volcanic cinder cone in southeast Portland—gives the adult derby a real slope and a distinctive local landmark.

The event fits a broader Portland tradition of unusual public spectacles, where creativity often matters more than strict competition; this year's field included a Zamboni (the machine that smooths ice rinks) and the Flintstones' foot-powered car (a nod to the classic cartoon Stone Age family).
Unlike children's soap box derbies that emphasize engineering and speed, the adult version treats the hill as a stage for humor, found materials, and absurd themes.
The result is a community block party where thousands of people can cheer for hours without needing to understand high-tech racing—only the jokes and the downhill chaos matter.

perspectives.description: Builders like John Nurse and Brittany England treat the race as a chance to turn silly ideas into moving sculptures and enjoy a supportive crowd. They see the loose rules and funny themes as the whole point.

A more traditional racing fan might argue that the event lacks the careful engineering and fair competition of youth derbies. The emphasis on pageantry and humor can make it feel less like a sport than a moving costume contest.

The race continues a national soap box tradition from the 1930s but reinterprets it for Portland's local culture. Its survival since 1997 shows how old customs can change when a community decides style matters more than speed.

The event may continue to grow as an alternative to expensive, high-tech motorsports. If it remains cheap, playful, and loosely regulated, it could inspire other cities to create similar low-stakes community festivals.
